extracted.intended_audience: artists, writers, and art critics interested in aesthetic theory and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts prescriptive aesthetic principles and practical critical standards for creating and judging art and literature, as argued in Wilde's dialogues and the accompanying art-criticism examples. Useful for writers, painters, and critics seeking rules-of-thumb for style, subject, and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art never expresses anything but itself
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art never expresses anything but itself. It has an independent life, just as Thought has, and develops purely on its own lines.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art is not necessarily realistic or spiritual in any given age; it does not reproduce its age but preserves the history of its own progress. It may revive antique forms or anticipate future appreciation; critics err when they pass from the art of a time to interpreting the time itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: All bad art comes from returning to Life and Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “All bad art comes from returning to Life and Nature, and elevating them into ideals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life and Nature may be used as rough material but must be translated into artistic conventions. If Art surrenders its imaginative medium (i.e., becomes mere transcription), it surrenders everything. As a method, Realism is called a complete failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid modernity of form and subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: “The two things that every artist should avoid are modernity of form and modernity of subject-matter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subjects not of one's own age; the modern tends to become old-fashioned quickly (example: Zola painting the Second Empire). Romanticism is said to be ahead of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life imitates Art rather than Art imitating Life
rubrics_metrics.description: “The third doctrine is that Life imitates Art far more than Art imitates Life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life's imitative instincts and its aim to find expression mean that Art offers beautiful forms through which life realizes energy. This theory reframes the history of art and implies artists shape cultural perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: External Nature also imitates Art
rubrics_metrics.description: “It follows ... that external Nature also imitates Art. The only effects that she can show us are effects that we have already seen through poetry, or in paintings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as both the secret of Nature's charm and the explanation of its weakness: our aesthetic perception of nature is mediated by artistic precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lying — telling beautiful untrue things — is the proper aim of Art
rubrics_metrics.description: “The final revelation is that Lying, the telling of beautiful untrue things, is the proper aim of Art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilde argues for cultivating the 'lost art of Lying' so that imagination and romance return; imaginative falsity (beautiful untruths) is an artistic virtue rather than deception to be condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge a work by laws deduced from itself; test internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: “I hold that no work of art can be tried otherwise than by laws deduced from itself: whether or not it be consistent with itself is the question.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should evaluate a piece on its own internal rules and coherence rather than by external standards or historical context alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art appeals primarily to the artistic temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art’s first appeal is neither to the intellect nor to the emotions, but purely to the artistic temperament.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The initial and central audience of art is the cultivated artistic sense or taste; intellectual or emotional arguments are secondary. Cultivation of taste (through exposure) produces sound judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste is perfected by frequent contact with the best work
rubrics_metrics.description: “This temperament, this ‘taste,’ as he calls it, being unconsciously guided and made perfect by frequent contact with the best work, becomes in the end a form of right judgment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated exposure to high-quality models trains judgment; fashions may still influence taste, and time (e.g., 'fifty years’ toning') often settles a work's merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key pictorial qualities to seek: composition, dignity of line, colour richness, imaginative power
rubrics_metrics.description: “The qualities that he sought for in a picture were composition, beauty and dignity of line, richness of colour, and imaginative power.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond mere accuracy, painters should prioritize these qualities; examples praise Turner/Constable for transcending mere transcription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the obvious and commonplace; resist mere transcription/topography
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objection: landscape as 'simply an enumeration of hill and dale... little more than topography.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique disfavors works that are only descriptive lists of observable details; successful art transforms material into deeper imaginative shapes rather than copying surface facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical mastery of colour, balance, and echoing tones
rubrics_metrics.description: Tintoret passage: robes and backgrounds are 'relieved' and 'beautifully echoed' in lower keys—demonstrating deliberate colour-balancing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical control over hue relationships, echoes, and balances is a criterion for visual excellence; critics may discuss glazing, broken tints, or morbidezza as valued terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indistinctness/veil to invite imagination; avoid over-clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: On Rembrandt: 'it would have lost nearly all its charms in losing that perplexing veil of indistinctness which affords such ample range wherein the doubting imagination may speculate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving some ambiguity or atmospheric indistinctness can be a deliberate aesthetic choice that enhances imaginative engagement; hyper-clarity can diminish poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archaeological accuracy and avoidance of anachronism in stage and scene design
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'strongly upheld the necessity for archæological accuracy in costume and scene-painting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In theater and historical representation, careful research and avoidance of anachronisms matter; linked principle: 'whatever is worth doing at all is worth doing well.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonize beautiful things irrespective of age, place, or school
rubrics_metrics.description: He recognised 'the true harmony of all really beautiful things irrespective of age or place, of school or manner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decorative and curatorial practice should not aim at archaeological reconstruction but rather at aesthetic harmony across periods and styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: A style so gorgeous that it conceals the subject can be an achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: “To have a style so gorgeous that it conceals the subject is one of the highest achievements of an important and much admired school of Fleet Street leader-writers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornate, richly embellished style that foregrounds aesthetic surface over transparent reportage can be a deliberate rhetorical/artistic tactic—particularly in journalism; the passage also warns of its potential to bore or mask.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate visual or emotional impressions into a literary equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: He aims to 'translate those impressions into words, to give, as it were, the literary equivalent for the imaginative and mental effect' and to 'make a prose poem out of paint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and critics should attempt to render pictorial or sensory effects in language, creating prose that captures the imaginative charge of visual art.
